Paris travel advice episode: User asked about city transportation and food recommendations. For transportation: Metro is best for getting around Paris; recommended Navigo Découverte card or weekly carnet of tickets for convenience; walking is viable in central neighborhoods like Marais and Saint-Germain; taxis/Ubers useful late at night but can be pricey during rush hour. For food must-tries: croissants and pain au chocolat from local boulangerie (avoid airport/train station vendors), proper French lunch at local bistro (soup, quiche, croque monsieur), crepes from stands in Montmartre, French cheese and wine at fromagerie, pastries like éclairs or tartelette from patisserie. Key advice: avoid tourist-heavy restaurants with street hawkers; walk a few blocks from main attractions to find locally-packed establishments for authentic cuisine.

User is trying to recreate their grandmother's apple pie recipe. I provided a classic recipe with: Filling - 6-7 cups sliced peeled apples (Granny Smith/Honeycrisp mix), 3/4-1 cup sugar, 2 tbsp flour, 1 tsp cinnamon, 1/4 tsp nutmeg, 2 tbsp butter, lemon juice. Crust - 2.5 cups flour, 1 cup cold butter, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp sugar, 1/2 cup ice water. Bake at 425°F for 45-50 minutes. User asked about a "secret ingredient" their grandmother added for rich flavor. I suggested vanilla extract as most traditional, also mentioned cardamom, allspice, apple cider vinegar, or maple syrup as alternatives.

User had two separate craft-related questions in one session. First, they asked about pie crust shrinking when baking - assistant provided troubleshooting advice: keep butter cold, don't overwork dough, chill shaped dough 30+ minutes before baking, don't stretch dough when fitting into pan, use pie weights for blind baking 10-15 minutes before adding filling, and avoid opening oven frequently to prevent temperature changes. Second, user asked about getting into hand-stitched leather crafts (wallets and belts) - assistant recommended starter tools: sharp knife or rotary cutter, edge beveler, sandpaper, leather needles (flat-bodied), waxed thread, stitching chisels or pricking irons, rubber mallet, and cutting mat.

Leatherworking tool advice: Skip stitching pony and clam initially - stitching pony is for bigger projects (wallets/belts can be held by hand), clam is for edge stitching on larger items. Save money for quality hand tools. Brand recommendations: Tandy's LeatherCrafter for beginners (reasonable prices, decent quality); Weaver Leather for mid-range; Keiffel, Badalassi Carlo, Rockler for higher-end investment. For stitching chisels, English point chisels from Spring Knifemaking are recommended, or start with inexpensive ones from AliExpress and upgrade later.

Leatherworking starter kit budget: $80-150 total for quality tools. Start with basics ($40-50): good knife, leather, needles, and thread. Add chisels and beveler later. Advice: avoid cheap tools as they frustrate and ruin leather. Recommended suppliers: local Tandy store (best for first purchase - can see/feel tools, get advice), Rocky Mountain Leather Supply and Oak Leaf Leather online, Amazon for basics like needles/thread. Avoid no-name bulk tool sets on eBay due to inconsistent quality.

Leatherworking guidance: For wallets, use 3-4oz leather (1.2-1.6mm) - thin enough to fold, sturdy enough to last. For belts, use 8-9oz leather (3.2-3.6mm). Start with vegetable-tanned leather as it's easier to work with and sands/bevels nicely; avoid chrome tan when learning as it's slippery and harder to edge. Tool maintenance tips: Keep knives sharp using a strop with compound regularly - dull knives are dangerous and tear leather. Oil chisels occasionally in humid climates to prevent rust. Store needles in a magnetic pin dish or wax paper. Maintain a dry environment to extend tool life.
